segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, together with all the holy ones who are in the whole of Achaia:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which is at work in the endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and our hope for you is firm, since we know that as you are sharers in the sufferings, so also in the comfort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, of the affliction that came upon us in Asia: we were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of living.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we would not rely on ourselves but on God, who raises the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He rescued us from so great a death, and he will rescue us; on him we have set our hope that he will rescue us yet again,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as you also join in helping us by your prayer, so that from many people thanks may be given on our behalf for the gift granted to us through many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is our boast: the testimony of our conscience that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and all the more toward you, with holiness and sincerity from God, not by fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are writing you nothing other than what you read and indeed understand, and I hope that you will understand completely,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as you have also understood us in part: that we are your boast, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With this confidence I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second favor,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to go on by way of you to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and be sent on my way by you to Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when I wanted this, I was not being fickle, was I? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there is both Yes, yes and No, no?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as surely as God is faithful, our word to you is not Yes and No.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you through us, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, did not become Yes and No; rather, in him it has become Yes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For however many the promises of God are, in him is the Yes. That is why through him also the Amen is spoken by us to the glory of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the one who makes us firm, together with you, in Christ, and who anointed us, is God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who also sealed us and gave the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I call on God as witness, on my own life, that it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that we lord it over your faith; rather, we are fellow workers for your joy, for by faith you stand firm.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints', which many translations keep, now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Others render it 'God's people'.

The Greek noun and its verb occur ten times in verses 3 to 7 and cover comfort, encouragement and strengthening appeal. The traditional 'comfort' is kept throughout the passage so that the repetition is audible. It should be heard as active strengthening as well as consolation, and some translations prefer 'encouragement'.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. 'Brothers' is the traditional rendering, and many recent translations have 'brothers and sisters' for the same reason.

This is the Roman province of Asia in the west of modern Turkey, whose leading city was Ephesus, not the continent. What happened to Paul there is not known. Suggestions include mob violence, imprisonment or a grave illness.

The Greek is literally 'from many faces', which may simply mean 'persons' or may picture faces turned upward in prayer. The sentence is also loosely built. 'Through many' may go with the gift, as here (granted in answer to the prayers of many), or with the thanksgiving (thanks given by many).

The manuscripts are divided between 'holiness' (hagiotēti) and 'simplicity' or 'straightforwardness' (haplotēti), two words that look very alike in Greek. SBLGNT reads 'holiness' and is followed here. Many translations and commentators prefer the other reading as better suited to the context, and the question remains open.

The Greek phrase can mean 'to the end' (in time, until the day of the Lord) or 'fully'. The contrast with 'in part' in the next verse favours 'completely', but both senses may be in play. The verbs 'read' and 'understand' also sound alike in Greek, a wordplay English cannot reproduce.

The word is the one translated 'grace' elsewhere in the chapter; here it means the kindness or benefit of a visit. 'Second' most likely refers to the two visits planned in verse 16, one on the way to Macedonia and one on the way back. Some manuscripts read 'joy' in place of 'favor'.

In Paul 'flesh' often means human nature left to itself, with its ordinary self-interested motives, not the body or sensuality in particular. The question is whether he plans as people usually do, saying yes and no as it suits him. 'Fleshly wisdom' in verse 12 has the same sense.

The Greek plays on two related words: God makes believers firm in Christos ('the Anointed One') and has 'anointed' (chrisas) them. 'Makes firm', 'sealed' and 'down payment' in verses 21 and 22 were all also terms used in commercial and legal transactions for guaranteeing a deal.

The word is a commercial term, borrowed from Semitic, for a first payment that secures a transaction and obliges the payer to pay the rest. 'Down payment' is the nearest modern equivalent; the older 'earnest' is no longer understood, and 'guarantee' loses the idea that part has already been paid. The Spirit is itself the payment: literally 'the down payment of the Spirit'.

candidates.reason: The noun and its verb παρακαλέω range over comfort, encouragement, exhortation and appeal across the whole New Testament, and translations vary widely; a sense-by-sense policy is needed.
The καυχάομαι word group is frequent in Paul and is rendered variously as boast, glory, pride or exult; readers lose the thread if the English shifts.
The plural addressed to mixed communities occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and the choice between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters' should be made once.
Paul's use of 'flesh' and 'fleshly' for merely human nature and motives recurs across the letters, and translators split between 'flesh', 'human' and 'sinful nature'.
It occurs three times (2 Corinthians 1:22, 5:5; Ephesians 1:14) with the same sense and is variously rendered earnest, pledge, guarantee, deposit or first installment.
